extracted.intended_audience: academic medical center public-relations staff, science communicators, health journalists, and researchers studying press release quality
extracted.subtask_short: academic medical center press release review
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist/rubric for evaluating the quality and accuracy of press releases issued by academic medical centers about biomedical research. Focuses on disclosure, quantification, design labeling, conflicts, and appropriate caveats to prevent overstatement and misleading pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal-to-human flag
rubrics_metrics.description: If the underlying study used animal models or in vitro cells, the release must say so prominently in the headline or first sentence and not silently imply human relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not imply human applicability when work is in animals or cells; explicitly label model system in headline/lead. Woloshin & Schwartz found 44% of releases promoted animal or laboratory research and 74% of those claimed relevance to human health despite no human testing — an anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Total N (and N per arm if randomized) belongs in the lead paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report absolute sample sizes up front so readers can judge study power and generalizability. Omission is common (23% of human-research releases omitted study size) and can falsely inflate perceived robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect-size quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Both relative and absolute effect sizes should be reported; do not claim 'increased' or 'reduced' without numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numeric effect sizes (absolute risk differences, rates, or means) alongside any relative measures and avoid language-only claims. Woloshin & Schwartz note 34% of releases failed to quantify results — a major source of misleading interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study-design disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label study design (e.g., RCT, observational cohort, case-control, retrospective, single-arm pilot, or in vitro).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make study design explicit in the lead so readers understand strength of evidence and causal inference limits. Mislabeling or vague descriptions can lead to over-interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and conflict-of-interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding source(s) and investigator financial conflicts should be disclosed at the top, not buried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State funders and any investigator financial ties prominently (lead or near-lead). Burying COI/funding reduces transparency and can mislead about motives or potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator-quote restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes should not contain interpretive claims that exceed the data; co-authors should review release quotes before issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hyperbolic or speculative investigator quotes that assert broader implications than supported. Woloshin & Schwartz judged 29% of releases to exaggerate importance and 26% of investigator quotes to overstate importance — require internal review and editing of quotes to match data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translational caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: For early-stage findings, the release must include a one-line caveat about the path-to-clinic distance (e.g., 'This is an early-stage finding; clinical application would require [N] more years of testing.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state how far the research is from clinical use (preclinical, pilot, preliminary) and, where reasonable, give an estimated timeframe or next steps. This prevents implicit promises of imminent human benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce the published paper's limitations section verbatim or present it in a lay summary; do not omit limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include study limitations (biases, sample restrictions, measurement issues) clearly and early. Omitting limitations was a frequent failure mode; including them helps journalists and readers assess credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication / consensus context
rubrics_metrics.description: State whether this is the first study, a replication, or one of many; describe what the broader evidence base says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place findings in context of prior work — single small study vs. consistent body of evidence — so readers understand whether results are preliminary or confirmatory. Lack of context can inflate novelty claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost / availability disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For interventions, state cost (where known) and availability (e.g., FDA-approved, in trials, lab-only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether an intervention is commercially available, investigational, or purely experimental, and include cost information if relevant. This prevents readers from assuming immediate access or affordability.
